content.text: {"primary_meaning":"A covenant most commonly signifies a solemn, binding relationship established by God, grounded in divine promise and often involving human obligations, signs, and communal identity. In Christian interpretation, the biblical covenants organize God’s redemptive relationship with humanity and Israel and culminate in the new covenant associated with Jesus Christ.","primary_basis":["Genesis 9:8–17 — God’s covenant with Noah, marked by the rainbow","Genesis 15:1–21; 17:1–14 — God’s promises to Abraham and the sign of circumcision","Exodus 19:3–8; 24:3–8 — the Sinai covenant between God and Israel, ratified with blood","2 Samuel 7:8–16; Psalm 89:3–4, 28–37 — the covenant promises concerning David and his royal line","Jeremiah 31:31–34 — the promised new covenant, including forgiveness and the law written on the heart","Luke 22:20; 1 Corinthians 11:25 — Jesus identifies the cup with the new covenant in his blood","2 Corinthians 3:4–18 — contrast between the old and new covenants","Hebrews 8:6–13; 9:15–22; 10:15–18 — Christ as mediator of the new covenant"],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"Covenant is understood chiefly as a contract or treaty: a formal agreement defining mutual commitments, blessings, and sanctions.","basis":["Deuteronomy 28–30 — covenant blessings, curses, and obligations","Joshua 24:14–28 — covenant renewal expressed through pledged commitments","Exodus 24:3–8 — formal ratification of the covenant"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Covenant is treated as a testament or divinely enacted disposition, emphasizing an inheritance secured through death, especially in interpretation of the new covenant.","basis":["Luke 22:20 — the new covenant in Jesus’ blood","Galatians 3:15–18 — covenant or testament language connected with promise and inheritance","Hebrews 9:15–17 — covenant language explained through the analogy of a will or testament"],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"Covenant functions as the comprehensive framework of redemptive history, often expressed in covenant theology through theological covenants such as redemption, works, and grace.","basis":["Genesis 2:15–17; Hosea 6:7 — often cited concerning a covenantal arrangement with Adam","Genesis 3:15 — interpreted as an initial promise of redemption","Galatians 3:6–29 — continuity of the Abrahamic promise through Christ","Hebrews 8:6–13 — transition to the new covenant"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"The biblical covenants are distinct historical administrations whose promises, especially those concerning national Israel, should not be absorbed into one overarching covenantal system.","basis":["Genesis 12:1–3; 17:7–8 — Abrahamic promises","2 Samuel 7:12–16 — Davidic promises","Jeremiah 31:31–37 — the new covenant addressed to Israel and Judah","Romans 9–11 — Israel’s continuing place in God’s purposes"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"Covenant is symbolized primarily through marriage, portraying God or Christ as the faithful spouse and the covenant people as the bride.","basis":["Hosea 2:16–20 — covenant restoration described as betrothal","Ezekiel 16:8–14, 59–63 — God’s covenant with Jerusalem depicted matrimonially","Ephesians 5:25–32 — Christ and the church interpreted through marriage","Revelation 19:7–9; 21:2–3 — the marriage of the Lamb and the bridal city"],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":true,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is broad consensus that covenant denotes a solemn, binding relationship or commitment, usually divinely initiated. It is not merely a symbol in the narrow sense but a major biblical-theological category. Considerable disagreement remains over whether covenants are primarily unconditional promises or bilateral arrangements, how the biblical covenants relate to one another, and the degree of continuity between Israel and the church."}
